title: Iran Just Stopped Two More Ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic Through the World's Most Critical Waterway Is Down 52%.
excerpt: The IRGC says it fired warning shots at two vessels overnight. Only six ships transited the strait on Sunday — the lowest in five weeks. An Indian crew member is still missing. And one ADNOC tanker is heading for India's Dahej port with no LNG behind it.
body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards fired warning shots at two ships attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz overnight Sunday into Monday, state television reported — the latest in a rapidly intensifying campaign to assert control over the waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil once flowed freely.

"Two ships that were attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz illegally were targeted and stopped by warning shots fired by the navy of the Revolutionary Guards," an IRGC correspondent told Iranian national television from near the strait. Iran did not identify the vessels.

The incident came hours after Iran attacked the Cyprus-flagged container ship GFS Galaxy on Saturday, striking it with a drone that caused significant engine room damage and forced the crew to abandon ship. Of the 24 crew members, 23 were rescued by the Omani Navy. One Indian national — identified as the ship's third engineer — remains missing. Cyprus's Deputy Ministry of Shipping confirmed Monday that a search operation is underway as the damaged vessel is towed toward the UAE port of Khor Fakkan.

## Traffic Down 52%

Ship-tracking data from MarineTraffic and Kpler now paint a stark picture. Vessel activity through the Strait of Hormuz declined approximately 52% between July 10 and 12 compared to the previous week. On Sunday alone, only six vessels transited the strait — the lowest number in five weeks.

Most tankers that did cross switched off their transponders while in the waterway, shipping data shows — an extraordinary measure that underscores how dangerous the passage has become for commercial shipping.

Among the ships that exited was the Very Large Crude Carrier Humanity, carrying two million barrels of Iranian oil, and the Capetan Andreas with 500,000 barrels of Kuwaiti oil products. Three empty tankers entered the Gulf to load oil. But notably, no liquefied natural gas tankers were visible entering the strait over the entire weekend — a worrying sign for gas-dependent economies including India, which relies on Qatari and Emirati LNG for its power grid and fertiliser plants.

One tanker controlled by Abu Dhabi National Oil Company exited the strait between July 10 and 12 and is heading for Dahej port in Gujarat — India's largest LNG import terminal. Whether more will follow is an open question.

## A Battle for Control

The duelling claims over who controls the strait have become the central fault line of the conflict. Iran declared the waterway closed on Saturday and says passage requires permits from its newly created Persian Gulf Strait Authority. The U.S. says Iran "does not control the strait" and that "traffic is flowing," with American officials reporting around 20 vessels escorted through in 24 hours — though ship-tracking data tells a different story.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran is seeking to establish a joint mechanism with Oman to manage strait traffic, adding that U.S. pressure on Oman had hindered discussions. The IRGC warned that "continued interference could lead to greater incidents in the global oil and gas sector."

The United States, which revoked its licence waiving sanctions on Iranian crude sales last week, launched another wave of strikes Sunday, hitting dozens of targets at multiple locations. U.S. Central Command said the strikes were "at the direction of the Commander in Chief" and aimed at degrading Iran's ability to attack civilian mariners.

## The War Has Widened

What began as tit-for-tat strikes has expanded to engulf the entire Gulf. Iran says it has targeted U.S. military facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, destroyed radar systems in Oman, hit fuel tanks at Jordan's Prince Hassan Air Base, and targeted a jet maintenance centre in Qatar. Bahrain confirmed its air defences intercepted Iranian missile and drone attacks early Monday.

The U.S. military has struck more than 300 Iranian military targets over the past week, including air defence systems, coastal radar, missile and drone capabilities, and small boats. Explosions were heard Monday in the Iranian port city of Bandar Abbas on the Strait of Hormuz and on nearby Qeshm Island, Iranian state media reported.

At least 20 people have been killed by renewed U.S. strikes in the past week, according to state media reports and official Iranian statements.

## What It Means for India and the Diaspora

India has nine merchant vessels with nearly 200 Indian seafarers stranded near the strait, according to the Ministry of External Affairs, which is maintaining close contact with Iranian authorities and shipping operators. The fate of the missing Indian crew member from the GFS Galaxy has become a point of national concern, with the Indian embassy in Oman coordinating search and rescue.

For the nine million Indians living and working across the Gulf, the widening of the conflict to Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, and Jordan is no longer a distant threat — it is overhead. India's oil imports face mounting disruption; the Dahej-bound ADNOC tanker is one of the few to make it through. Brent crude rose more than 2% on Monday, adding to the pressure on Indian fuel prices, remittances, and the broader economy at a moment when India was beginning to see the Gulf crisis ease.

The ceasefire that briefly calmed the region last month is now formally dead. For Indian families sending money home, Indian sailors navigating the world's most dangerous waterway, and Indian businesses that depend on Gulf trade routes, the question is no longer whether the conflict will escalate — it is how much further it will go.

*Sources: Reuters, Kpler shipping data, MarineTraffic, Cyprus Deputy Ministry of Shipping, Iran state media, U.S. Central Command*
